content.title: About
content.content: Pig's feet are the meat and gelatin obtained from the lower limbs of a pig. They are rich in collagen, have a deep meaty flavor, and develop a slightly jelly‑like texture after long cooking. They are commonly used in stocks, stews, braised dishes, and as appetizers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pig's feet contain a large amount of gelatin that turns into a rich broth when simmered slowly.
In many traditional cuisines (e.g., Russian, Polish, Chinese) pig's feet are considered a delicacy and feature in festive meals.
Collagen from pig's feet is often processed into food‑grade gelatin used in jellies and desserts.
When cooked properly, the meat becomes tender enough to melt in the mouth.
Pig's feet are frequently served cold after marinating in vinegar and spices.

items.title: Rich in collagen
items.content: Collagen supports skin elasticity, joint health, and connective‑tissue repair.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and tissue maintenance.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Contains iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for blood health, immunity, and bone strength.

items.title: Glucosamine and chondroitin
items.content: These compounds, present in the cartilage of the feet, may aid joint function.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Suitable for low‑carb diets when prepared without added sugars.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Pig's feet can be fatty, so people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Potential pathogens
items.content: Improper cooking may leave bacteria such as Salmonella; thorough heat treatment is required.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Those prone to gout should limit intake due to purines.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Feet are usually boiled or braised for several hours until tender, used in stocks, soups, stews, or marinated in vinegar with spices. After pre‑cooking they can be roasted in the oven to develop a crispy crust.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh pig's feet in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Before cooking, inspect for off‑odors or discoloration and discard if present.
